cited_details.statement: Person search aims to find a probe person from a gallery of whole scene images and has significance in the video surveillance field for tracking lost people, re-identification, and identity verification, with direct relevance to public safety and social governance (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imavis.2020.103970).
Image-based person search matches a probe image against a gallery of whole scene images (http://www.ee.cuhk.edu.hk/~xgwang/PS/dataset.html).
Text-based person search retrieves a target pedestrian by a natural-language query without requiring a visual probe (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/56e3758cd9acc97f41ed3dbefd66fd76f238e4fb).

Three core challenges recur across both subfields: (1) learning discriminative deep feature representations; (2) bridging the gap between query and target through deep metric learning with novel loss functions; and (3) mitigating inconsistencies between detection and identification tasks (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imavis.2020.103970).

The CUHK-SYSU benchmark was released to support end-to-end person search research, comprising 18,184 images, 8,432 identities, and 99,809 annotated bounding boxes across hundreds of scenes (http://www.ee.cuhk.edu.hk/~xgwang/PS/dataset.html).

proposed a deep learning framework that jointly handles pedestrian detection and re-identification in a single convolutional neural network rather than as two separate stages, and introduced an Online Instance Matching (OIM) loss to train the identification branch under sparse and unbalanced labels (https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850).

The CUHK-SYSU project further showed that jointly optimizing these two objectives in a unitary process outperforms baselines that simply combine a pedestrian detector with a re-identification model (http://www.ee.cuhk.edu.hk/~xgwang/PS/dataset.html).
A subsequent study explored an end-to-end model trained sequentially on the CUHK-SYSU or PRW datasets (https://cea.hal.science/cea-03251768/document).
*2.2 Deep metric learning (Theme 2).* The OIM loss is the loss function proposed to train the identification branch of the joint detection-identification framework (https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850).

To address the limitation that OIM treats all samples equally and ignores hard samples, a Triplet Online Instance Matching (TOIM) loss was proposed that combines the advantages of OIM and triplet loss while simplifying batch construction (https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10560).

A 2020 survey of the field explicitly identifies deep metric learning with novel loss functions as a major focus of recent image-based person search work (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imavis.2020.103970).

*2.3 Discriminative feature representations and stated limitations.* A multi-level feature fusion model for person re-identification combines global and local features of pedestrian images to learn more discriminative representations (https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4893/13/5/111).

The 2020 person search survey lists low resolution, pose variation, background clutter, occlusion, viewpoint changes, and low illumination as persistent open challenges for deep-learning-based person search (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imavis.2020.103970).
The TOIM paper additionally notes that triplet loss converges slowly, which motivated the hybrid OIM-triplet formulation (https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10560).

*3.1 Discriminative feature representations (Theme 1).* A deep adversarial graph attention convolution network (A-GANet) exploits object properties and relationships from scene graphs of both queries and gallery images to learn informative textual and visual representations (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/56e3758cd9acc97f41ed3dbefd66fd76f238e4fb).

For cross-modal text-to-image matching more broadly, adversarial representation learning was introduced to learn discriminative embeddings that explicitly account for the large word variance in the textual input (https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10534).
Early work constructed a benchmark for natural-language person retrieval and developed an attention-based system to localize a described person in an image (https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08923).
Deep reinforcement learning was also investigated as a mechanism for natural-language person search (https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00365).

*3.2 Bridging the query-target modality gap (Theme 2).* A-GANet bridges the modality gap by adversarial learning, using a feature transformer and a modality discriminator to learn a joint textual-visual feature space for cross-modality matching (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/56e3758cd9acc97f41ed3dbefd66fd76f238e4fb).
match the distributions of features belonging to the same identity across the two modalities as the mechanism for measuring cross-modality distance (https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10534).

*3.3 Stated limitations.* Attention-based natural-language person retrieval recognizes that the task is challenging because language semantics are latent and hard to quantify, alongside visual challenges such as low resolution, deformation, and occlusion (https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08923).

A-GANet is evaluated on the CUHK-PEDES and Flickr30k benchmarks and demonstrates effectiveness for cross-modality pedestrian matching (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/56e3758cd9acc97f41ed3dbefd66fd76f238e4fb).

In the image-based setting, the joint detection-identification CNN with the OIM loss is a canonical response to the inconsistency between detection and identification objectives (https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850).
Hybrid losses such as TOIM extend metric learning to emphasize hard samples (https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10560).

In the text-based setting, adversarial graph attention networks jointly address discriminative feature representation and cross-modality alignment (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/56e3758cd9acc97f41ed3dbefd66fd76f238e4fb).
Adversarial representation learning targets the large variance in textual inputs (https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10534).
Persistent open issues include robustness to low resolution, occlusion, and illumination in image-based search (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.imavis.2020.103970).
The quantification of language semantics for text-based retrieval remains a further open issue (https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08923).
